wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.notes: A few steep moves off a broken ramp system past a tree to a ledge belay.
Thin-hands splitter crack, then step left around a pillar to a stance.
Stem a thin, slabby corner up to a large treed ledge.
A corner (5.10b right, 5.8 left) leads to a finger-and-thin-hand crack in a dihedral; some parties split this into two pitches.
Short traverse left under the huge roof to a crack anchor; often wet after rain.
Hand crack in a corner past a roof to the crux boulder-problem moves — the route's namesake crux, well protected despite the grade.
Flakes and jugs lead into a flaring chimney widely regarded as the region's hardest 5.8, then a hand crack on a clean slab.
Move right along a ledge system and simul-climb easy ground toward the summit block.
A short, exposed boulder-problem move gains the top of the balanced summit block; many parties fix a toprope for the second.

wa_flight_of_the_falcon.notes: The route is reached over the base of Roan Wall. From the thin boulder-filled watercourse below the wall, climb the obvious bolted 5.8 slab at the toe of the small buttress; it is the same first approach pitch used by the Roan Wall routes.

Scramble a short way up the gully, then climb the dirty low-fifth-class crack/groove on the right side of a brushy wall to reach the foot of Roan Wall. The crack holds moss and dirt and is noticeably worse when wet.

From the foot of Roan Wall, scramble up along its left side to the saddle left of the wall, where Salish Peak comes into view, then cross the high basin to the toe of Salish's south face. Brush in the basin is often soaking in the morning.

Start at the very toe of the steep south face, a little left of its lowest point; the line trends left overall. The 5.10b crux is a well-bolted face section, and like every 5.10 section on the route it can be pulled through on the bolts if needed.
Traverse left at the bolt just off the belay, then follow an enjoyable 5.9 ramp system. There is a detached block on this pitch; climb around it with care. Views open up toward Three Fingers.
One of the route's two named crux pitches: a slabby 5.10b face section protected by closely spaced bolts. Mixed gear and bolts elsewhere on the pitch; the belay is bolted.
A short, powerful 5.9 layback is the feature of this pitch; belay at a bolted anchor.
A splitter 5.9 finger crack on clean granite. Belay at the bolted anchor above.
The crux of the route: face climbing up a green-tinted slab on solid rock, well protected by bolts. Grades given for it range from 5.10b/c to 5.10c.
Climb to the Falcon's Perch, an exposed stance above a roughly 500 ft drop to the base. This is the last bolted anchor on the route and the usual place to start rappelling with two 60 m ropes.

Optional continuation toward the summit. Rock quality drops off noticeably above the Falcon's Perch and there are no bolted anchors; protection is there but has to be looked for. Test holds and build belays from natural gear.

Easy fourth-class to about 5.2 ground to the summit of Salish Peak; some parties unrope for it. From the top, the walk-off leads back down to the base, an easier option than rappelling from the summit.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.notes: A rambling, typical alpine first pitch through moss, some loose rock, and vegetation to a tree anchor partway up the gully.
A crack system winds through ledges past some loose 'kitty litter' rock to the base of the route's large dihedral.
Climbs the dihedral through a bulging roof; the crux move is protected right at your waist by a good #4 cam before easier climbing ambles 60 ft to a tree ledge.

The route's technical crux: 20 ft of 5.8/9 leads into a ladder of roughly 14 closely-spaced bolts (5.10+/A0), finishing with face moves and a finger crack; free climbers link it around 5.11a. Hanging belay off two bolts with chains.
Traverse right clipping bolts to a beautiful finger crack that takes solid jams and gear, easing to 5.7 near the belay.
A right-leaning crack with sketchy gear gives way to a second bolt ladder with two mandatory 5.9+ free mantle moves (aid at A0); ends at a bolted belay.
One hard move pulling off the belay ledge, then a wandering, well-featured crack system with sparse gear to a tree anchor.

Rambling ledges, cracks, and trees lead to a big ledge; skip the mossy slab above by trending left on a ramp to a final unprotected easy slab at a bolted anchor right on the east face's edge -- a spectacular, exposed top-out.
An exposed step-down off the last anchor onto a small ramp leads to easy terrain and the true summit; most parties simul-climb or solo this short finish.

wa_southern_man.notes: Shares the Direct East Buttress's rambling, sometimes-loose first pitch through moss and vegetation to a tree anchor.
A shared crack system with the Direct East Buttress winds through ledges to the base of the large dihedral.
Climbs the shared dihedral through a bulging roof, well protected at the crux move, before easier climbing to a tree ledge.

Where the Direct East Buttress heads up its bolt ladder, Southern Man breaks out left instead onto an awkward 5.10a section, leaving the shared line about halfway up the wall on the way to its own south-facing headwall.
First headwall pitch: sustained 5.10 finger and hand cracks on excellent rock, with the odd-numbered headwall pitches generally the more straightforward crack climbing.
The route's crux: a short, bulgy face section with bad feet above thin pro; the FA party aided this at 5.9+ C1 in 2008, freed at 5.11d in 2010.
More sustained 5.10 crack climbing continues up the headwall with the same excellent finger locks found on the pitch below.
A harder, cruxier face-climbing pitch linking crack systems; belays on this upper section are reported as vague and unfixed, so build gear anchors with care.
The final headwall pitch eases to sustained but comfortable 5.10- crack climbing, topping out near the summit and the standard South Arete descent.
